title: AI Can Prep Your Case. It Can't Save You at the Lectern
author: Fitzy
source: Teaching in the Age of AI on Substack, December 8, 2025
summary: Fitzy has coached and judged middle-school debate for fifteen years, and this piece is the clearest classroom-adjacent field report on AI's effect on student thinking that Tim's archive has picked up so far. The setup is the format itself: students get the topics a month out, prep freely, but do not learn which motion or side they will argue until twenty minutes before the round, then transcribe notes onto colored paper with no screens allowed in. The format was designed pre-AI to reward deep preparation while still requiring understanding. It turns out to be a remarkably effective stress test for AI-assisted prep. The observation is damning and specific. In the 2020s, minutes with an LLM produce a structured case, anticipated rebuttals, and polished language. On tournament day, students furiously copy AI-generated text onto their colored sheets, filling both sides. The old tournament hum of students arguing, explaining, and passing notes is replaced by near-silence. In rounds, arguments converge to a common median because they all draw from similar training data. Sixth graders attempt strict-scrutiny arguments about the First Amendment but cannot pronounce constitutional. Cross-examination exposes the gap immediately: students repeat scripted phrases or scrutinize their paper hoping an answer appears. The piece's sharpest reframe is that debate, unlike classroom submission, has no one to cheat but yourself. There is no teacher grading, no delay between performance and feedback. The judge, the opposing team, and spectators watch in real time. AI can write your speech; it cannot deliver it, pivot under a point of information, or synthesize a debate that has actually unfolded. The silver lining is that the activity rewards the students who did the work anyway. For Tim, the generalizable move is that public-speaking assessment formats (debate, mock trial, Socratic seminar, oral defense) become structurally more authentic as AI reshapes written work, because no AI can fake live understanding.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Instead of the wacky variety of MS arguments and exuberant buzz of the “prep” period, I encountered homogenized cases and near-silence as students furiously copied word for word from pre-canned AI debate language onto colored sheets of paper, the only permissible material allowed into the round.

In the debates themselves, many students struggled to pronounce words they had never used and make arguments they didn’t understand. Although they appeared more prepared than ever before, detailed note sheets covered with text, in reality many could not articulate a coherent response in the face of any kind of rebuttal.

In fall 2025, within minutes of opening an LLM, any MS student with even rudimentary prompting skills can generate a sophisticated case with solid arguments, detailed evidence, and clear structure. The AI will anticipate counterarguments and provide rebuttals.

While creating cases is exactly what debate preparation is supposed to produce, the process is supposed to take weeks, the result of hard work and earned knowledge. When there’s literally no effort required to generate detailed arguments, all the worst aspects of using AI come into play.

What I observed across multiple rounds Saturday was striking sameness. Almost all the arguments were identical, the same three points on each side, the same evidence cited, the same structure, because it was all being drawn from the same pool of training data.

One motion involved First Amendment issues. I watched three sixth graders attempt highly sophisticated constitutional arguments (strict scrutiny!) when it was clear they couldn’t pronounce “constitutional”, let alone explain what the First Amendment actually protects.

AI can write your speech. It cannot deliver it. It cannot answer a point of information from the other team. It cannot pivot when you’re presented with an unexpected argument. It cannot respond in real time as the debate evolves.

That’s why I think public speaking activities, debate, Model UN, mock trial, speech competitions, will become increasingly valuable as AI continues to transform education. Assessment formats that require oral defense of claims and arguments are even more authentic than in class written work.” Archived from Teaching in the Age of AI on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
